newsitem.title: USA: Republicans call on Clinton to enter tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Republicans call on Clinton to enter tax talks.

text.p: The Senate's top Republican said on Sunday that President Bill Clinton must personally take part in the final round of budget and tax talks if the two sides hope to clinch a deal by their Aug. 1 deadline.
Saying a final deal was "close and yet we're so far away," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott told NBC's "Meet the Press" the president needed to meet with him and House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

As the president prepared to play golf in Los Angeles, the White House said he was "fully engaged" through his negotiating team which included Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin. "At the appropriate time he would be willing to get personally involved in the talks," presidential spokesman Joe Lockhart said.

The White House said last week that the president was ready to give up his scheduled August vacation in Martha's Vineyard, Mass., to finish up the tax and spending deals. Congressional Republican leaders have said they want to strike a deal before leaving for vacation August 1.

Clinton's team also includes Budget Director Franklin Raines, Economic adviser Gene Sperling and congressional liaison John Hilley. They and congressional Republican leaders met Saturday but talks stalled when they were unable to resolve outstanding issues -- child tax credits, child health care benefits, Medicare premium increases for the affluent and capital gains taxes.

"We're at a point after a meeting ended last night about 6:30 (2230 GMT) where the president needs to step in and say 'yes, this is important, we're not going to use this for political position, we're going to do what's right for the country," Lott said.
"If the president will do that, if he'll join with us, we can make it happen. But right now, we're so close and yet so far away," the Mississippi Republican said.

House Majority Leader Dick Armey signalled that Republicans may be willing to give in on one of their top issues -- indexing of capital gains tax rates to save investors from paying tax on profits due to inflation -- in order to get a tax bill Clinton will sign into law.

"We understand that in order to get some of the other things that may not be something to hold up," Armey, a Texas Republican, said on ABC's "This Week." "I'll have a chance next year with another tax package to maybe pick up those pieces that get lost behind in this one," he added.
Raines, appearing on "Meet the Press" repeated the president's view that indexing of tax rates would lead to a veto of the entire tax cut bill.

Administration officials and top Republicans, led by Gingrich and Lott have closeted themselves in a private third floor meeting room of the Capitol out of bounds of the press in order to hammer out a deal. Most Democrats, including House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota, have not been included in the negotiations.

The White House and Republicans are trying to bridge differences in plans to give taxpayers an $85 billion tax cut over the next five years and make changes in domestic health social programmes to balance the budget by 2002.

In one move over the weekend that opened a door to compromise, Republicans were considering acceptance of one item on Clinton's wish list -- a tax credit for low income workers who pay federal payroll taxes but not income taxes.

Republicans have said the president must accept both the tax cut and spending bills. With their main priority the tax cut, they do not want to risk the president signing off on the spending bill and vetoing the tax cuts.
"We can safely think on the tax side that nothing will be agreed to until everything is agreed to," Sperling told reporters Saturday.
